title: No Bids. No Calendar. No Clarity. Indian Football's Premier League Is Fighting to Survive.
excerpt: AIFF heads to the Supreme Court as ISL faces an existential crisis after the commercial tender draws zero bidders and the Master Rights Agreement expires without replacement
body:
The Indian Super League was supposed to be the vehicle that would drive Indian football into the modern era. Eleven years after its launch, the league cannot confirm whether its next season will happen.

The All India Football Federation is preparing to approach the Supreme Court of India this week to seek modifications to the constitutional framework that governs the federation. The ISL has been omitted from AIFF's official calendar for the 2025-26 season. Not a single entity bid for the league's commercial rights when the AIFF issued a Request for Proposal. The Master Rights Agreement between AIFF and Football Sports Development Limited, which has run the ISL since its inception, expired in December 2025 with no replacement in sight.

This is not a scheduling hiccup. This is an existential crisis.

## How the Money Dried Up

The MRA, signed in 2010 for a fifteen-year term, granted FSDL full commercial control over ISL in exchange for an annual payment of ₹50 crore to AIFF. When the agreement expired, the AIFF launched a tender process for a new commercial partner, setting a minimum guaranteed fee of ₹37.5 crore per year.

No one bid. Not one.

The market's silence was a verdict. After a decade, ISL clubs have haemorrhaged money. Several franchises have paused operations. Player salaries have been delayed. Contract renewals have stalled. Foreign players have left for leagues with more certainty. The commercial model that was meant to professionalise Indian football has instead exposed the sport's fragile economics.

The Supreme Court has compounded the paralysis. A standing directive prevents AIFF from signing any new commercial contracts until a judgment on its constitutional validity is delivered. The next hearing is scheduled for July 14 — by which time preseason would traditionally already be underway.

## The I-League Fills the Vacuum

With ISL's status in limbo, the I-League — India's original top division, which was demoted when ISL took primacy — is the only confirmed senior men's football league for the 2025-26 season. It is scheduled to begin on October 19 in a compressed, eighty-day format designed for survival rather than spectacle.

The symbolism is difficult to miss. A league built to replace the I-League may now be the one that disappears first.

AIFF President Kalyan Chaubey has said only that "all decisions will be taken in the best interest of Indian football." Behind the rhetoric, contingency plans are being drawn up on both sides. FSDL could seek a six-month transitional extension to complete one more ISL season under interim arrangements. But that would require agreement from clubs, broadcasters, sponsors, and the federation — a consensus that appears unlikely in the current climate.

## The FIFA Shadow

India's football governance has drawn FIFA's attention before. In August 2022, the AIFF was suspended by FIFA after the Supreme Court installed a Committee of Administrators to run the federation, an act deemed "undue third-party influence." The suspension lasted ten days — lifted only after the CoA stepped aside and elections were held.

The current situation is more complex. The draft AIFF constitution, prepared by Justice L. Nageswara Rao, contains progressive reforms: a fourteen-member Executive Committee with at least five former players (including two women), an age cap of 70 for office-bearers, and reduced voting power of state associations. But the delay in implementing these reforms has created the very administrative vacuum that now threatens the ISL's survival.

Should the constitutional impasse persist, FIFA and the AFC retain the authority to suspend AIFF again — which would strip India of participation in international competitions and further damage a footballing ecosystem already on life support.

## What Diaspora Fans Stand to Lose

For the Indian diaspora, ISL has been an imperfect but real connection to Indian football. It has been broadcast in the US, UK, and Canada. It has featured players of Indian origin from abroad. It has given diaspora fans a league to follow, argue about, and invest emotion in — something that Indian football historically never offered.

If the ISL collapses — or emerges from this crisis as a diminished, austerity-era product — that connection frays. The diaspora's engagement with Indian football, which was never as deep or as assured as with cricket, could retreat to the margins for another generation.

The next Supreme Court hearing on July 14 will determine not just the ISL's future, but whether Indian football can sustain the institutional architecture it needs to compete. The stakes are not theoretical. They are on the docket.
